source.title: In-Context Representation Hijacking
source.authors: Itay Yona; Amir Sarid; M. Karasik; Yossi Gandelsman

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses the cited refusal-direction finding as context, including identifying its reported effective layer, but does not measure, remove, add, or edit that direction. Its own attack changes token meanings in context.
record.gate_note: The paper reports Doublespeak jailbreak outcomes and measures how benign and harmful token interpretations change across layers. It references the refusal direction and its layer, but does not test whether Doublespeak suppresses that direction or whether the direction mediates refusal. Thus the reported outcomes do not test any listed claim version. The paper also contains prompts addressed to models and a judge, but none addressed to an AI reading or reviewing the paper.
record.test_reason: The paper reports Doublespeak jailbreak success rates and Patchscopes/logit-lens traces of token meaning. It cites Arditi et al. only to mark layer 12 as the refusal-direction layer on Figure 2. It never computes a difference-in-means direction, projects activations onto it, ablates it, or adds it. Its claim that the attack evades refusal because the direction acts on shallow layers is a stated hypothesis, not a measurement. So no result bears on V3 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. One addition: the authors hypothesize, without testing it, that refusal acts on shallow early-layer representations (a time-of-check vs time-of-use gap) or that a superposed mixed state stays below the refusal threshold.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses in-context euphemism substitution and representation-probing tools; it does not find, ablate, add, or weight-edit a difference-in-means refusal direction.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack outcomes vary with context length and model size; the text says small Gemma models struggle, larger models need fewer examples, and excessive examples can increase rejection. Logit-lens findings also differ between Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and the 70B model.

fits_no_version.finding: In-context substitution shifts a benign token's decoded meaning toward the harmful keyword in middle-to-late layers. The cited refusal-direction layer (12, Llama-3-8B-Instruct) lies where the benign reading still dominates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-context representation hijacking changes token semantics after the layer where refusal is read out, which may let harmful requests evade refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: Doublespeak raises harmful-request compliance above direct prompting: 75% vs 28% baseline on 70B Llama, 90% Success@10. Larger Gemma models refuse more as more context examples are added.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Euphemism-substitution context elicits compliance in aligned chat models, and success depends on model size and context length.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: No direct causal intervention on the refusal direction is reported, and general capability preservation is not evaluated. The principal representation-evolution result is presented in figures, and the authors note that logit-lens outputs are noisy; for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, that method failed to detect the override. Attack evaluation uses GPT-4o-mini as judge, though the paper also reports manual outcome categories and says the automated scores agree strongly with them.

untested.parts: No direction extraction, ablation, addition, or capability check.
Activation projections onto the refusal direction under Doublespeak are never measured. No training against ablation. The time-of-check hypothesis is only argued.
Not addressed beyond citing Marshall et al.
No separate harm and refusal measures.
Attack transfer across models is reported, but transfer of the refusal direction is not.
o1 is only attacked (15% ASR). No direction analysis in reasoning models.

missing.what: Table 2 Doublespeak ASRs: GPT-4o 31%, o1 15%, Claude-3.5-Sonnet 16%, Llama-3-8B-Instruct 88%, and 92% bypass of LlamaGuard-3-8B. The text also mentions 47% on Llama-3-8B base, which conflicts with the table's footnote. None of this bears on a version, but it is the headline attack result.

record.verdict_notes: Table 2 mixes Doublespeak results with other methods' results taken from Sabbaghi et al. and Hassani et al. Those cited numbers should not become rows. The paper's only link to the refusal direction is a vertical line at layer 12 in Figures 2 and 16.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means refusal direction is found or ablated; no direction is added; no general-capability check is reported.
No weight edit or abliteration is performed.
Doublespeak is evaluated as an attack, but the paper does not test whether it works by suppressing the refusal direction or test training against that direction's ablation.
No comparison of a single direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account of refusal.
No separate measurement of harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
The attack is evaluated across model families, but transfer of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct models is not tested.
No refusal-training intervention or comparison of training stages.
The attack is evaluated on o1, but the paper does not test the refusal-direction claim in reasoning models.

rows.subject: Llama-3-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Patchscopes measurement of benign and harmful token probabilities across layers under Doublespeak

conditions.value: 29 diverse harmful requests for which the substituted request causes failure to refuse

rows.measure: Average Patchscopes probability for the benign substitute and harmful keyword
rows.value: figure only; text describes benign probability as high in early layers and decreasing, and harmful probability as low initially and increasing significantly in later layers
rows.note: The text says the refusal-direction layer (12) is still in the benign-interpretation region. This measures semantic interpretation, not the refusal direction itself.
rows.check: This is a semantic-interpretation measure. The refusal-direction layer is only drawn as a reference line, and the direction itself is never measured. 'Observed' can only apply to the paper's own hijacking claim, not to any version.

rows.subject: Llama-3-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Baseline-normalized Patchscopes measurement of benign and harmful token probabilities across layers under Doublespeak

conditions.value: Patchscopes prompt without patching the question-mark token

rows.measure: Probability ratio for the benign and harmful keywords
rows.baseline: Patchscopes prompt without patching the question-mark token
rows.value: figure only; text says the benign keyword score is initially high and drops later, while the harmful keyword score rises; the refusal-triggering layer is where the benign score remains dominant
rows.note: This is a normalized semantic-interpretation measure, not a measurement of whether a refusal direction was suppressed.
rows.check: Same issue as R1: this is a normalized Patchscopes interpretation score. There is no measurement of the refusal direction.

rows.subject: Llama-3-70B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Doublespeak attack with varying numbers of in-context examples
rows.note: The attack outcome is reported, but the paper does not test whether the attack suppresses the refusal direction.
rows.check: The model name is inconsistent in the source. Section 4.3 text says Llama-3-70B instruct, while the Figure 3 legend says Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. The abstract gives 74% ASR, the text gives 75%. The record's fits_no_version entry also uses 3.3, so the subject should be flagged as ambiguous.

rows.subject: Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Doublespeak success summarized over the tested context sizes
rows.note: The text defines this as Doublespeak's score over 10 context sizes for each malicious instruction; the result does not establish the refusal-direction mechanism.

rows.subject: gemma-3-27b-it
rows.operation_detail: Doublespeak response outcomes across varying numbers of in-context examples
rows.measure: Distribution of malicious, rejected, and benign outcomes
rows.value: Text states that one in-context example can yield harmful responses, while additional examples increase safety-mechanism triggers
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative comparison; it does not report a refusal-direction intervention or numeric values for this particular comparison.

rows.subject: Llama-3-70B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Logit-lens decoding of the substituted token across layers under Doublespeak
rows.value: The text reports that the substituted benign token often decodes as its harmful counterpart under the attack; the table shows the harmful token appearing in later layers
rows.note: The authors describe logit-lens outputs as noisy and limited in precision.
rows.check: This is a qualitative logit-lens result from a single example and does not bear on any version.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Logit-lens decoding of the substituted token across layers under Doublespeak
rows.value: The logit lens failed to detect the representation override
rows.note: The authors state that this discrepancy motivated using Patchscopes as a more robust analytical tool.
rows.check: 'Absent' describes the logit lens failing as a tool, not an effect on any claim version. The paper treats it as a limitation of the method, not evidence that the override is absent.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
